Take a look at sentiment right now.

Because of a personal event involving Jensen Huang, there are now widespread calls that the "AI bubble has popped."

Sentiment is as though AI has failed, the investment wave is over, and we are in a global depression.

In reality? The S&P 500 is up +7% YTD, +60% in 5 years, and ~7% away from a record high, with US AI CapEx running at over $1 trillion per year.

Meanwhile, AI-associated sectors and tech investments have accounted for ~44% of total US GDP growth on a rolling four-quarter basis.

And, Nvidia, $NVDA, is guiding nearly $750 billion in revenue for next year, even without Jensen Huang.

The underlying fundamentals of the AI Revolution have not suddenly deteriorated because of a leadership crisis at one company.

The unfortunate result of this drawdown, as with nearly every other correction since the AI Revolution began, will be countless investors getting crushed on the way back up.

Today's fearmongers become tomorrow's short squeeze as soon as sentiment shifts again.

The comments on this post will be a perfect example of just how polarized sentiment has become in the "doom" direction.

Asset owners will win and the AI Revolution is far from over.

tweets.text:
Be careful chasing coins tied to narratives that are dependent on news and headlines.

e.g. have seen a lot of people chasing GTA VI coins

one of the most popular narratives has been what the name of the in game currency will be

the issue with this type of narrative is - the in game currency will have NOTHING to do with any of the memes being made about it...

the only people who will initially be interested in stacking a meme about it instead of stacking the actual in game currency itself are already trading it

could a winner eventually pick up more steam as the trenches as a whole pick back up?

sure!

but odds are - most events like this in this type of market end up being sell the news and require a decent amount of distribution and time before they continue to send higher

if you're fine with that and want to try and nail the exact top of the narrative, no worries

gl & godspeed

tweets.text:
Imo @metricxyz is one of the most promising things in the DeFi space rn and I was happy to contribute to this research from @schemacap

Here's your TL;DR ↓

Metric = onchain DEX that can compete with Binance on execution despite having much less liquidity.

1) Capital efficiency

Metric processed $1.01B in trading volume with just $7.12M in average liquidity across 12 stock pools in 20 days.

That's ~141x its deposited capital.

2) Liquidity model

Metric uses liquidity bins that follow stock prices, while curators manage trading strategies.

This keeps liquidity near the market price, so LPs don't have to constantly reposition their funds.

3) Metric vs. @Binance

Metric: better execution in 76/87 completed $100K stock sell comparisons (after Binance's standard trading fee)

Binance: better coverage for larger orders

4) Metric vs. @PancakeSwap

For $10K NVDA buys, Metric offered better execution in 70/73 comparisons, which comes out to ~$17 cheaper per order (median).

5) Metric vs. @Uniswap V4

For $100K META trades on @RobinhoodCrypto Chain, Metric's median quoted execution cost was just 4.4 basis points, compared to Uniswap's 93.5.

Next Hyperliquid here?

tweets.text:
On the bright side, capital flowing from other sectors + semis to a successful $ANT IPO...

will eventually flow back into semi balance sheets over the long run. Circle of life. but for semis.

If we look at Anthropic's $900.9B of eventual purchase agreements:

- $AVGO + financing partners: $161.2B in Google TPU leases
- Google Cloud: at least $121.3B
- SpaceX: Up to $120.5B (ceiling, can be cut)
- Amazon: at least $110B
- Microsoft: $47.2B-$49.2B
- Nscale:  up to $44.6B
- Lambda: ~$41.3BN ($34.9B can be cut)

With other identifiable counterparty deals such as:

- $MU (undisclosed), but supply agreement
- $RIOT: ~$28B+ $9.1B
- $WULF: ~$19B
- Akami: ~$11.6B (CPU cloud)
- Volta: ~$10B
- OnePWR: ~$3.4B
- $CRWV (undisclosed)
- Everwind (undisclosed)
- Likely $IREN (undisclosed)
- Zerra DC (undisclosed)

Outside the $900.9B, there's another:

- Additional Google TPU capacity: $125B-$150B estimated

- $AMD: over $20B if Anthropic takes the full initial tranche of Helios capacity

I'm actually personally longer term bearish on frontier lab valuations (I like OpenAI more if I had to pick one due to consumer stickiness). But raising a lot from IPO does help raise their counterparty status.

Regardless of how they utilize it, that's a lot of GPUs, TPUs, HBM, optical networking, and compute needed for the next 5+ years.

tweets.text:
Now that we're close to 2027 it's a good idea to stress test downside scenarios where you have:

1. Capex cuts past 2028 
2. Stranded Compute / DC Slowdowns 
3. Finance deterioration (base case)
4. 2x+ rate hikes

Working in parallel and see what happens with valuations of AI longs. 

If you see acceleration despite all 4, I'd argue that's an opportunity. 

> Next-gen of photonics is one of the rare segments with an extreme rise in optical content and ASPs that can offset aggregate capex cuts. 

Everyone’s moving into that space, including Elon Musk doing M&A, Marvell, Samsung and others with M&A… and we haven’t seen economic impact on emerging architectures even hit players from Celestial to Ayar + their suppliers yet. 

If we look at a scenario where there's excess GPUs but power constraints:

We might see slowdown in aggregate accelerator/GPU/ASIC procurement, but your optical engines + light sources + switches players see acceleration.

Especially as incentive to replace power inefficient networking... since different (cheap BOM) optical architectures improves GPU utilization or even HBM requirements.  

So value migrates to players more high-beta to architectural shifts. 

If Celestial projections are $500m -> $1B, and we expect -30% aggregate capex cuts, I'd argue we'd still see upward revisions from Celestial over the next 2 years.

But financing with #3 matters a lot as seen with $AAOI dropping off of a $550M, vs. $COHR getting prepayments for capacity expansion from their customers. 

Companies that rely on external foundries might be less sensitive to #3 since they're not as capex intensive. 

On the other hand, companies in sectors have a lot of floating interest like certain Neoclouds, and require further financing might be the most impacted. 

> Legacy and specialty memory is a different cycle that markets conflate with AI capex.

If consumer demand weakens but at the same time, players like Windbond exits DDR2, pricing durability is longer than markets expect. 

> Wafer/substrate procurement such as ABF, SOI, InP are low cost but large downstream destruction if not secured, so we’ll likely see acceleration here as seen with $NVDA earnings call. 

> qualification cycle players within bottlenecks remain very compelling, since first revenue in a large TAM, relative to MC is material to that company. 

If a company is valued at $400m then they get a $200m of orders, it's more asymmetrical to a certain company than a rounding error to a $50B incumbent revenue. 
_

There’s period of times where prices are dislocated from fundamentals from leveraged players getting wiped. I’d argue that time is now. 

I disagree with a lot of the stupid "it's over takes" but I agree it's a good idea to haircut future capex expectations and forward valuations due to financing tightening + macro. 

It's also good idea to see the nuances and stress test downside cases. 

But TLDR: I'd argue next phase of AI infrastructure is going to be increasingly disconnected from aggregate AI capex growth. 

I just personally wrote 4 things I'm using to stress test jointly some of the names I'm looking at, so I'm more comfortable waiting things out... despite seeing hedge funds getting liquidated left and right and overwhelming short positioning. 

I personally see acceleration in more narrow parts of the supply chain, while markets treat the entire AI trade as one.  

We'll see how things play out on longer horizons.

The Fed hiked for two years, and the private sector barely felt it. Washington felt all of it.

Corporate America and homeowners locked in record-low rates during the pandemic, so corporate interest costs as a share of GDP actually fell while rates rose. The federal interest bill went the other way, more than doubling from about $500 billion in 2020 to roughly $1.25 trillion today.

The cost of higher rates landed on the government, not companies or consumers. That is why tightening barely dented the economy, and why the debt is the real pressure point. Every rate the Fed holds high, the Treasury pays for.

#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper

Inflation is proving sticky. The dollar is near a 19-month high. Metals are feeling the squeeze.

🌎 MACRO
US retail sales rose 0.2% in October, while import prices jumped 1.1% versus 0.7% expected. That keeps pressure on the Fed to tighten. Williams favours further hikes, although he pushed back against more aggressive action.

UK inflation just climbed to 3.6%, but core inflation held at 2.8%. An uncomfortable headline, with less acceleration underneath.

Oil offers some relief: Brent slipped towards $92 after a reported US inventory build. Renewed US–Iran attacks and Hormuz shipping risks could still reverse that move.

☢️ URANIUM
The latest weekly update puts spot at $90.30/lb last Friday, versus a $97 term benchmark at October-end. Utilities are still evaluating offers. My focus remains on signed contracts and the prices needed to bring new supply online.

🥈 SILVER
Around $46 in early trading, down roughly 3%. Higher rate expectations are squeezing precious metals, while silver also carries exposure to industrial demand.

🥇 GOLD
Around $3,778, down nearly 2% and at its lowest since September 2025. A firm dollar and elevated yields are overpowering haven demand.

🔶 COPPER
A stronger dollar and tighter financial conditions remain headwinds. Watch whether physical buying strengthens as prices retreat.

👀 TODAY
Fed minutes at 20:00 CET, US housing data and official oil inventories.

My take: sustained relief in oil, yields and the dollar would give metals breathing room. Until then, strong balance sheets and funding visibility matter.

Long-term bullish. Short-term selective.

Follow @Swedish_Uranium for the daily metals pulse.

BTC fell 13% in three days.

Everyone has a theory for why: Nvidia, the Fed, the Anthropic IPO, MSCI, the midterms, the Binance hack.

I ranked all 6 by evidence (and two of them don’t hold up):

#1: Leverage, set off by the Nvidia news

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on Nov 12, and Nvidia dropped about 10% at the open.

BTC closed that day at $73,974, and three days later it was at $64,120.

What made it so fast was leverage. About $1.3B of leveraged BTC longs got liquidated on Nov 13 and 14, and every forced sale pushed the price a bit lower and knocked out the next batch.

I'm not sure Nvidia was the trigger, but the liquidations line up almost perfectly with the steepest part of the drop.

#2: The Fed is hiking again

The Fed hiked in September for the first time in about three years. Then October inflation came in hotter than expected (+0.4% vs 0.3%), and markets now see about an 85% chance of another hike in December.

When cash pays more, money comes out of risky stuff first. You can see it in the spot BTC ETFs, which had seven straight days of outflows from Nov 5 to 13, about $1.91B in total.

This explains why we're going down, but not why it happened so fast.

#3: Money being pulled out for the Anthropic IPO

Anthropic is raising up to about $64B and lists on Nasdaq this Thursday. Money that size has to come from somewhere, and some of it may be coming out of crypto.

Matt Cole pointed out that BTC did something similar before SpaceX's IPO in June. It fell into the listing, bottomed a few weeks later and then recovered.

The stablecoin drop fits this story too, but honestly it fits the other theories just as well. One past IPO is interesting, but it's not enough to call it proof.

#4: MSCI dropping Strategy from its index

Evidence: low to medium

MSCI is set to remove Strategy (MSTR) from its USA index after Nov 30. Index funds will have to sell MSTR, which makes it harder for Strategy to keep buying bitcoin.

That's a slow drag over time, so it doesn't really explain a 13% drop in three days.

The two theories that don't hold up

• The midterms: Democrats won both the House and Senate on Nov 3.
That's bad news for crypto bills, but BTC actually went up from $76,709 to $80,443 in the two days after.

• The Binance hack: $6.3B was stolen on Oct 29, and a week later BTC was still at $80,443.

There are three dates I'm watching:

• Nov 19: Anthropic lists. If #3 is right, the selling should ease in the weeks after.
• After Nov 30: MSCI's change kicks in.
• Dec 9: the Fed decides on rates.

What would make me more confident is stablecoin supply growing again and ETF flows turning positive.

If the ETFs are still bleeding by the Fed meeting, that points to the Fed, and that one doesn't fix itself on a set date.

I'm happy to bet 100k USD against this claim:

"AI can run most businesses better than humans now"

So to make it specific, I am making a bet that

- in next 6 months since today ("now")
- there is and will not be a single company
- that is fully managed by AI without human guidance (= no human oversight apart from first initial prompt/setup, it can hire humans to do work)
- and that generates recurring revenue for 3 months totalling 1M USD or more (I'd like to define business as an entity that makes money on ongoing basis, not just a one off event)
- by providing services or products to customers (which I consider to fall under "most businesses", e.g. I'd exclude market trading bots and exploit/hacking bots)

History says one more hike won't be enough.

Markets now price another Fed hike in December.

It has typically taken around 200bps of hikes to bring CPI inflation down by 100bps. In every hiking cycle since 1966 where we can date the inflation peak, nominal growth peaked first, typically about 8 months earlier.

Today: nominal growth is only just slipping below trend, and inflation is still broadening. This cycle has further to run.

I believe the @nvidia board is not acting in the best interest of shareholders nor in a manner consistent with their fiduciary duties. 

What we know is that the board fired Jensen or forced his resignation for violating company policy and/or in response to the accusation of an affair with a spy. 

They did so without careful consideration of the impact on the company, its customers, its shareholders or other stakeholders. 

They rushed to judgment without the benefit of careful due diligence or even with a basic understanding of the facts. 

How do we know this? 

We know this by how quickly Jensen was fired and how little was known at the time of his firing. 

It takes time to convene a board meeting.  There was time, maybe, for one Zoom. 

And this is a decision that should have been made by a board sitting in person and carefully deliberating the facts once they are known.  

And they should have slept on the decision and met again the day after to discuss the facts, the risks and the other implications of their decision. 

The timing and lack of information did not allow for careful board deliberation. 

While boards can fire a CEO for an inappropriate relationship with a subordinate, it should not be an automatic decision. That is why we have boards comprised of humans and not agents. 

A board should consider whether or not such a relationship was consensual or whether it was an abuse of power dynamics. And a board has to consider what the impact of the firing is on all stakeholders. 

If I were in this board, I would not have rushed to judgment based on articles in the media. I would have made sure the board had all of the facts so it could make a careful and informed decision. 

Boards of Delaware companies have a duty of care which means they must make informed, prudent and good faith decisions. This clearly did not happen here. 

What law firm is advising this board?  

Or is the board even taken good legal advice? 

It doesn’t look like it. 

And now the board is compounding its failures by insisting that there is no possibility for Jensen’s return as CEO. 

Why is it in the best interest of the company to foreclose the possibility of Jensen’s return and to do so before all of the facts are known? This is yet another breach of their duty of care. 

Furthermore, the board has launched an investigation whose scope is unknown. Investigations can be extremely damaging to a company and should be carefully targeted to address whatever facts need to be known rather than be overly broad in scope. 

In short, this looks like a series of major governance failures by directors that panicked due to headlines in the media. They likely felt compelled to do something because they were afraid of looking bad in the media, not because it was the right thing for them company. 

They couldn’t stand the heat. 

The board’s conduct here is shocking for a company of this scale and importance to our country and the world at large, particularly at this moment in history.

The difference with $ZIM is that it holds roughly its entire market cap in cash.

Other companies can report fantastic earnings, but if market sentiment is weak like the current environment, there’s very little they can do to support their stock price.

$ZIM is different. If the stock falls, management has the financial firepower to launch massive buybacks or pay substantial dividends.

Currently, the buyout restrictions limit their ability to do so, although shareholders are still expected to receive roughly a 20% dividend yield.

Once their hands are untied from this ridiculous buyout offer, they can aggressively repurchase shares if the market continues to undervalue the business.

That’s what makes $ZIM different. It doesn’t have to rely entirely on market sentiment to create shareholder value.

This is why I consider it one of the safest investments in the stock market, with an exceptional risk-reward profile.

The difference with $ZIM is that it holds roughly its entire market cap in cash.

Other companies can report fantastic earnings, but if market sentiment is weak like the current environment, there’s very little they can do to support their stock price.

$ZIM is different. If the stock falls, management has the financial firepower to launch massive buybacks or pay substantial dividends.

Currently, the buyout restrictions limit their ability to do so, although shareholders are still expected to receive roughly a 20% dividend yield.

Once their hands are untied from this ridiculous buyout offer, they can aggressively repurchase shares if the market continues to undervalue the business.

That’s what makes $ZIM different. It doesn’t have to rely entirely on market sentiment to create shareholder value.

This is why I consider it one of the safest investments in the stock market, with an exceptional risk-reward profile.

I just listened to a Stanley Druckenmiller interview. You can find the link below. I think it’s fantastic, and I highly recommend studying it and writing down the investment lessons.

One thing that stood out to me was his discussion of hot and cold streaks, something I’ve become increasingly aware of in my own trading.

Looking back, I was extremely hot during the first three quarters of this year. In the fourth quarter, I started getting colder.

The mistake wasn’t getting colder. That’s inevitable. The mistake was recognizing it, watching my P&L deteriorate, and still continuing to play big instead of reducing my position sizes, trading less, or focusing only on my highest-conviction opportunities.

One of the most important skills in investing is knowing when to press your advantage and when to step aside. Your P&L often tells you before your ego is willing to listen.

Honest take on the AI Nuremberg trailer from someone who has been pretty resistant to AI film

The Good:
+ Amazing imagery, worldbuilding and translation of the lore, if you know it
+ Insane 1 person can do this and the visual/audio editing makes me hyped for the film, first time feeling that
+ Huge reduction in cost compared to previous tech (CGI etc) to render and create entire new worlds, even if all film doesn't go this way, a new industry will be born around it
+ the marvel/netflix-ification of cinema means we've already got a ton of human made slop that is no better than this now. So complaints purely directed at it being derivative fall flat
+ This still needed someone who knew the lore, picked the shots and timed the edit. That's the impressive part
+ Overall insane how far we've come from Will Smith eating spaghetti

The Less Good/Skeptical:
- A lot of what makes it work is lifted from recent films (1917 visual, boots from 28 years later) which is closer to a collage than inspiring something new. Whether AI can ever truly do that is another question*
- It's a trailer. Mapping that out into a film that not only makes sense but is engaging is infinitely harder and a different skillset
- Most complaints about AI content are dialogue and characters. It's hard to judge that as there is none of that here. Ultimately it's what films live or die on

Overall I'm super impressed. Especially given the speed of the improvement in AI, but it's worth pointing out that is all it is for now - a trailer, and the parts missing are exactly where AI has been weakest so far

I will see it if it's made. Out of sheer curiosity if nothing else. Which says a lot about how far it's come

Extraordinary numbers for a company trading at… CASH.

The reason you don’t beat the indices is that you’re scared shitless when Nasdaq volatility ($VXN) hits 40 or the $VIX hits 35, precisely when you should be buying aggressively.

Instead, you’re afraid to buy $NVDA at $160 and dump your tech stocks after they’ve already fallen 50%.

That’s where real contrarian investing comes from. Buying when everyone else is terrified. That’s how you beat the indices.

Just remember, all the stories about the future are theories. Most will never materialize. Your fears are just fears, not facts.

I can almost guarantee that a few years from now, you’ll look back at $NVDA trading at $160 and say, “It was so obvious.”

Not in one month, four months, or six months. I’m talking about a few years.

The market rewards those who can think in years while everyone else is panicking about the next few weeks.

tweets.text:
All the business school curricula need to be rewritten for the 21st century.

Good corporate governance should be defined as founder control, with dual class stock, not board control. The board is just an advisory board. The shareholder vote is a backup in the event of issues, and shareholder sales are the extreme backup.

This should be obvious from the financial performance of founder-led global tech companies vs manager-led incumbents. And also obvious in terms of just how much value these boards typically consume rather than produce.

After all, typical board members aren’t like execs that a CEO can actually assign tasks. Instead, they have power, and often time to scheme amongst themselves, but lack true operating knowledge of the underlying company. The exception is when there are real founders on the board themselves — but those are exceptions.

To be clear, the 20th century MBA-style corporate governance playbook was actually fine for the era of General Mills, General Motors, and General Electric. In that time period, the individual didn’t matter that much. They didn’t have the leverage that computers give them.

But now the Internet has obsolesced all that. So YC, Founders Fund, and a16z are much better business schools than Harvard Business School, which is culturally obsolete because it is technologically obsolete. The world it was implicitly premised on no longer exists.

However, all these intuitions and best practices, the conventions that built billion and trillion dollar companies, have only been informally advocated in blog posts and contracts. To change the defaults, we’ll need to actually write a new curriculum.

As I do after every quarter, let me share the snapshot of the overall digital advertising industry.

Some key takeaways from 3Q’26:

Digital advertising industry decelerated from 20.2% in 2Q’26 to 16.1% in 3Q’26. As mentioned in my last quarter’s snapshot, given the tough comp I expected both Q3 and Q4 to experience deceleration.

Meta’s incremental share jumped to 52.7%. Outside the ATT-distorted 2022 numbers, this is the first time in this snapshot that $META captured more than half of the incremental dollar. There is a bit of an asterisk here. $AMZN moved Prime Day into June this year, so its ad growth slowed from 26% in 2Q’26 to 11% in 3Q’26, which mechanically flatters everyone else’s incremental share. If I combine 2Q and 3Q, Meta’s incremental share was ~48%. That is still comfortably ahead of its ~35% current share, so the share gain story remains fully intact even after adjusting for the Prime Day timing.

$GOOGL Search’s incremental share dropped to 27.6%, the lowest since 2Q’23 (which was again distorted by ATT). Last quarter I wondered whether Search could hold ~30% incremental share or would drift toward the mid-20s. But we need to adjust for the Prime Day impact here as well. On a combined 2Q and 3Q basis, Search’s incremental share was just a tad bit below 30%. Let’s wait a couple more quarters to see if $GOOG Search can stay around this level or keep drifting downwards.

As a reminder, the actual digital advertising industry is larger than what my snapshot below shows, but this snapshot helps me gauge the broader digital advertising industry’s big picture. TikTok and Walmart advertising are notably missing here. Well, TikTok is a private company and Walmart doesn’t disclose their advertising revenue consistently.

full piece: https://t.co/gn5UBHLXnf

The frustrating part about the stablecoin drain is that the fix already exists.

Since 2022 stablecoin supply has moved inversely with T-bill yields (-0.62 correlation on 90-day changes). Rates aren't the only driver, but when bills pay more, stablecoins lose out because holders earn nothing.

Tokenised money market funds hold the same T-bills, pay you the yield & live onchain. In principle that makes them a better product than a stablecoin, and better than a traditional money fund too, as they can settle and be posted as collateral 24/7.

In TradFi, money funds grow when rates are high or markets are stressed, as people park cash. Onchain, they should be the offset when stablecoins shrink, but at $17.1B they're only 6% of stablecoin supply. Many of the big ones are for wealthy investors only (BlackRock's needs $5M, JPMorgan's $1M), and even the retail ones need ID checks, approved wallets and business-day redemptions.

Fix that and I expect this becomes one of the biggest growth areas onchain.

I think it will become extremely obvious that swarms of AI agents are the future of performance marketing.

AI works particularly well when outcomes are verifiable. And performance marketing is almost the perfect environment for that. You have CPC, CPM, CPA, conversion rates, ROAS, and ultimately the only metric that really matters: how much incremental profit each dollar of ad spend generates.

I’ve worked quite a bit with performance marketing agencies. It’s a very human-intensive business. You hire specialists for each channel, they come up with hypotheses, launch campaigns, test a handful of creatives, adjust targeting and bidding, analyze results, and repeat.

Now imagine a swarm of agents doing this 24/7, across every channel, running thousands or potentially millions of experiments, constantly generating new creatives, exploring audiences, reallocating budgets, and learning from actual outcomes.

It’s basically a giant closed-loop optimization problem with a measurable reward function.

And unlike many agentic applications where success is subjective, here the feedback signal is brutally clear: did the campaign generate more incremental profit than it cost?

The future of performance marketing looks a lot more like autonomous experimentation than traditional agency work.
